analysis.one_liner: Restores federal and local authority to regulate cable TV rates.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on May 15, 2001 and never received a vote, with 17 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1996 Congress stripped the FCC and local franchising authorities of their power to limit cable television rates. This bill would repeal that change and bring back the rate regulation rules that existed before 1996. It never advanced past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Cable subscribers, who would again be protected by federal and local limits on what cable companies can charge for basic service.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals section 301(b) of the Telecommunications Act of 1996, which barred the FCC and local franchising authorities from regulating cable television rates [S2].
Reinstates section 623 of the Communications Act of 1934, the cable rate regulation framework in effect before the 1996 law, effective 90 days after enactment [S3].
The sponsor introduced it explicitly to restore the authority of the FCC and local franchising authorities to regulate cable rates [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Cable television companies, which would once again face government limits on the prices they can charge, and would bear the cost of complying with rate regulation.

drawbacks.text: Price regulation can suppress the incentive to invest in cable networks at a time when the industry was building out infrastructure and facing new satellite competition; supporters of the 1996 deregulation argued competition, not rate caps, would discipline prices.
The bill simply revives the pre-1996 regulatory regime wholesale rather than designing new rules, so it inherits whatever flaws the old rate regulation had.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For households facing rising cable bills, restored rate regulation offers direct, tangible relief. The honest cost is that regulation can slow network investment and the bill takes a blunt approach by resurrecting old law rather than writing new rules. Still, the tradeoff runs toward consumers: the 1996 deregulation removed price protection for a service most households had little choice but to buy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Telecommunications subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended without ever coming up for a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Barney Frank introduced the bill on May 15, 2001, with Rep. James McGovern as an original co-sponsor [S3].
The House referred it to the Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S1].
A week later, on May 22, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Telecommunications and the Internet, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the Congress [S5].
It drew 17 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Cable television operators, who kept the deregulated rate structure Congress gave them in 1996 and faced no renewed price limits.

for.name: Rep. Barney Frank
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to restore FCC and local authority over cable rates.

for.name: Rep. James McGovern
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill with Rep. Frank.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it out; it also sat in the Telecommunications subcommittee from May 22, 2001 onward with no recorded action.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support recorded, and the Republican-run Energy and Commerce Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would have reimposed federal and local caps on the rates cable companies can charge, reversing the 1996 deregulation of their pricing. Cable operators benefit from charging subscribers unregulated prices, so their interest in this bill ran against the viewers they serve.
